Curated, evidence-driven (entries earn their place in eval rounds), and gated: declare-help.test.mjs asserts every synonym target resolves in the reference and every negative entry answers its trigger words. negative.answer: No app-facing bitmap cache or preload call. Today each `Image` instance decodes its `source` itself — a photograph shown on one surface is decoded again on the next. A platform-managed bitmap store (decode table shared across instances + cached draw rasterizations) is planned — see docs/system-design/ (adaptive draw cache) and the 2026-08-06 assessment; until it lands, the idiom is to keep the SAME view alive across surfaces (one sprung scalar, many followers) rather than to rebuild it.

No hooks, no stores, no props plumbing — state is an attribute declared where it lives (`count: number = 0` on a view), derived state is a `{ }` constraint reading it, and "effects" are the constraint graph's own propagation. A descendant reads an ancestor's attribute by name (`app.count`, `parent.width`, `classroot.…`) — no context, no lifting. Handlers write; constraints react.

No refs — a named member IS its handle (`box: View [ … ]` → `app.box`); reach any node by its dotted path. Replicated rows take their identity from the record's `id` field on their own, and `key = :field` on the replicated node names it when it lives under another name — that is Declare's `key`, an identity attribute, not React's reconciliation prop.

No SVG element — a vector mark is a `draw(d: DrawContext)` member (paths, arcs, gradients — a recorded, reactive drawing), the house icons are `Icon` subclasses drawn exactly that way, and an actual `<svg>` you already have lives inside a `DOMIsland`.

No grid layout strategy — `WrappingLayout` flows and wraps; a fixed N-column grid is a small `Layout` subclass of your own (`place()` is ~15 lines of arithmetic over `this.laid()` and `this.view.width`); and tabular DATA wants `Table` or `DataGrid`, which are classes, not layouts.

No ZStack and no overlay wrapper — children stack by default: a view with no `layout` imposes no arrangement, and declaration order is z-order (later siblings paint above). Place the layers with x/y; `ignoreLayout = true` floats one child above an arranged set.

No dedicated class — the library is deliberately small, and these are compositions: a skeleton is a few rounded Views whose opacity a `Time` pulses; a badge is a small rounded `Text` riding its parent's corner; an avatar is an `Image` with `stretches = cover` and rounding. Compose it, then keep it as your own class.

No `requestAnimationFrame`, and no timers: a body that names `setTimeout` or `setInterval` is refused. Motion is declared: a `Spring` drives an attribute toward a live target (interruptible for free), an `Animator` is the clock-shaped sibling, and per-frame integration (physics you step yourself) is `Time [ tick = frame, onTick(dt) ]`, which rides the one shared frame clock; a value that is a function of the current time — a clock face, a countdown — derives from a `Time` member's facts (`now`, `minute`, …). One call on the next frame is `afterDelay(0, fn)`. See the guide's Motion and states chapter.

No polling — nothing waits. A program never checks whether something has happened yet: readiness is a value to constrain on, completion an event to take — a loop or timer that checks whether something has happened yet is a constraint or an event written by hand, and almost always the wrong path. Ask what it is waiting for: a fetch landing → `visible = { data.loaded }` or `onLoad`; a view existing or having a size → `onInit`, `onReady`, `afterSettle`, `onArrive`; a value changing → a constraint on it (the constraint IS the notification); geometry after your own write → `afterSettle(step)`, same frame. Time is only ever an input: `Animator` over a duration, `Spring` toward a target, a `Time` fact (`clock.minute`, `clock.now`) to derive from, `Time [ tick = frame, onTick(dt) ]` to integrate (a per-frame handler that ignores `dt` is polling), `afterDelay(ms, fn)` for a genuine timing rule — a debounce, a request timeout — never to let things settle. See the guide's Time and change events chapter.

No formatting functions of Declare's own: numbers, money and dates are formatted by the host's `Intl`, called from a `{ }` or a script function like any other global — `new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(1234.5)` is "$1,234.50", `(1234.5).toLocaleString("en-US")` is "1,234.5", and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` writes weekdays and months in the language it is given. Name the locale, and a `timeZone` for a date. Guide: docs/guide/12-text.md § Text. `Intl` is one of the globals every `{ }` body and handler may name; which globals code may name, by where it is written: declare-help globals.

No `<select>` element: a pop-up choice is a `Button` with a `menu`. Declare a `Menu` whose rows carry `checked`, derived from your state, and set the state in its `picked(id)`:
  sorts: Menu [ items = { [ ({ id: "name", label: "Name", checked: app.sort == "name" }), ({ id: "date", label: "Date", checked: app.sort == "date" }) ] }, picked(id: string) { app.sort = id } ],
  Button [ label = { "Sort by " + app.sort }, menu = { app.sorts } ]
The button draws the chevron and opens the menu under itself, and the menu checks the current row (declare-help Control.menu). Other ways to choose one of many: two to five short choices shown at once, `Segmented`; a few that need a sentence each, `RadioGroup`; a long list filtered by typing, `Combobox`; a day, `DatePicker`; your own content in a bubble, `Popover`. Guide: docs/guide/08-controls.md § Choosing one of many.

No host globals beyond a fixed set: what code may name depends on where it is written.
  Everywhere, `{ }` bodies and handlers included: the ECMAScript built-ins (`Math`, `JSON`, `Date`, `Intl`, `Number`, `String`, `Array`, `Object`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, `Promise`, …), and `URL`, `URLSearchParams`, `console`, `structuredClone`, `encodeURIComponent`, `decodeURIComponent`.
  Refused in a `{ }` body or handler, with the Declare way named: `fetch` (a `DataSource`), the timers `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `queueMicrotask`, `requestAnimationFrame` (`afterDelay(ms, fn)`, a `Time`), `performance` (a `Time`), `globalThis`.
  In a `script { }` block: all of the above, `fetch`, the timers and `performance` included.
  In a `script [ host = browser ] { }` block: `window`, `document` and the rest of the browser as well. An unmarked script runs on every host, so the compiler refuses them there.
What a page reads from `window` is an App attribute here: the size is `app.width` / `app.height`, and a view is reached by its name (`app.sidebar.list`), not by a query. docs/declare.md § 5.

No lookup function: a member is a property of its view, reached as JavaScript reaches any property — `toolbar.share`, or by a name computed at run time, `toolbar[name]`. The two forms are the same access and chain freely: `app.prefs[section][field]`, `app.prefs[section].advanced`. Each bracket steps one level; its string names one member, not a dotted path. The result is the member by that name, or `undefined` when there is none. A string literal (`toolbar["share"]`) is checked like a path; a name known only at run time cannot be, so a path stays the form for names known as you write. Data can name a view: `anchorTo = { app.toolbar[:target] }`. Guide: docs/guide/04-structure.md § A member by a name known at run time.
